title: How Forward Deployed Engineering is done at Kepler — Vinoo Ganesh
talk_summary: A Palantir-veteran talk arguing forward-deployed engineering is a product-discovery strategy, not a sales role: embed with users, find the real problem, ship the smallest fix, and generalize into product.

takeaways.what_they_do: Before building anything, ask what the user is trying to accomplish, what happens after, and how they solve it today; if the fix is under a day of work, just ship it and close the loop instead of expanding scope.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If solving the problem is under a day of work, just build it and ship it and close the loop.
takeaways.numbers: 47-page requirements doc and 3-month estimate collapsed to a 4-hour Slack alert

takeaways.technique: Detect repeated manual toil as work signals
takeaways.what_they_do: Watch for tasks done more than once, copy-paste between tools, tool/tab switching, and 'I have to' exasperation as hints of a real problem worth automating.
takeaways.evidence_quote: any task a user does more than once ... that is a pattern and a hint that there's a problem and an opportunity

takeaways.what_they_do: Define canonical nouns and verbs for overloaded terms (customer vs client vs org ID) so integrations and pipelines stop breaking on mismatched definitions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when you define the language, you control the narrative

takeaways.technique: Ship like it runs 18 months; no 'temporary' hacks
takeaways.what_they_do: Calibrate what ships by asking if you'll get a 2am call in 6 months, what the trade-off is, and who owns it after handoff; treat every hack as permanent production code.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Every hack goes into production ... you will be responsible to support that hack in perpetuity.
takeaways.numbers: A quick Groovy retention script survived 12 months and ran for a ~100,000-person customer
